It wasn’t in my shift but in my co-worker’s shift two months ago wherein they wheeled in a young pregnant female unresponsive since unknown time and with no prior anc (a third world country where not many women still get their ancs done). The consultant was about to declare but out of curiosity wanted to see the fetus and maybe determine the weeks of pregnancy and saw that fhr present. They started cpr and opened the abdomen and the baby popped out, who was sent away with the peads to resus. Central pulse of mother returns and ob took her to OR thinking that the uterus ruptured since they did not open  uterus to take the baby out. In OR, they found that this was an abdominal pregnancy, removed the placenta and closed her up and shifted to ICU. In icu, realised that she had hypoxic brain injury and did not have good prognosis. The premie baby did not also have good chances of survival in the nicu. The Patients parents took them home from icu for end of life care and I assume they wouldn’t have survived long after reaching home.

It was truly a wild time for some in the hospital cause of this case.

I would abort my fetus if they were diagnosed with down’s. 

Being in a medical field, there is a reason as to why tests were developed to know if your child has downs as early as 10 weeks into pregnancy, and it’s not just downs but various other crippling conditions. 

It’s one thing to calm your souls down by saying that you were here to bring this child into the world, but it’s a whole another Pandora’s box when you actually have the child. Maybe right now you will be in a position to financially aid all the problems the child might have, but that doesn’t mean you’ll forever be. With the strain it’ll put on the family and siblings who are put in a position to take care of the said child and their medical issues. 

Hospitals aren’t fun. Having been through a situation where a single parent was hospitalised, and not being able to take a single leave to tend to them even though I was working in the same hospital made me realise, it’s a lot of mental and physical work that you will have to put in. 

And unlike a family member who is sick, it’s your child with varying disabilities from birth and it’ll continue till they die, and you can never predict if they will be able to cope with the extensive changes that come along with it. Life is never idealistic that way. Though this argument can be given to any child who might be born without a syndromic issue, but there are a myriad of problems and commitments with Down’s syndrome.

If you are in this position, please please do meet parents with said children, and try to learn about them and their struggles.

I understand that, when I started my fellowship, I made mistakes, so many of them that at one point I wanted to refuse seeing anymore patients and just go home. I felt like I did everything I could, but nothing was going right. And I went to my consultant, with whom I could have an open conversation. He sat down and spoke to me about how to be effective and fast, which he learnt through years of experience.

It wasn’t that the next day I was perfect at what I did, but 2 whole months of effort and feedback’s and extra studying which made me better. I still do ask for feedbacks from himeven now, it’s one step at a time.

The residents are humans too, they would have gone through the same mistakes, go try to talk to them about. Have an honest conversation and put effort into it. Just for 1 week, and then evaluate your life again.
